title: H-1B Crackdown Widens as Trump Administration Targets OPT, Fees and Vetting Rules
excerpt: The administration proposes a permanent $103,265 H-1B fee, considers a similar charge for OPT, and has tightened scrutiny of applicants — pushing registration numbers down more than 25%.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed making the H-1B visa fee permanent at $103,265, up from the initial $100,000 executive order fee set to expire in September
  • A separate $100,000 fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT) — the program that lets international students work after graduation — is pending White House review
  • H-1B registrations have dropped more than 25% from 2024, with employers seeking about 344,000 visas compared to 794,000 in 2023
  • Hospitals, research institutions, and nonprofits would be exempt from the new fee under the proposed rule

The Trump administration is broadening its crackdown on work visa programs, moving beyond the initial H-1B fee increase to target the Optional Practical Training program, tighten applicant vetting, and propose making six-figure visa fees a permanent fixture of the US immigration system.

In a rule proposed this week, the Department of Homeland Security would set the H-1B visa fee at $103,265 — a permanent replacement for the $100,000 fee imposed by executive order last year, which is set to expire in September. The government projects the new fee would generate roughly $8.8 billion in revenue to fund the immigration system, including immigration courts that handle deportation cases.

OPT in the Crosshairs

The administration is also considering a $100,000 fee for Optional Practical Training, the program that allows international students to work in the US for up to three years after graduation on their student visas. The policy is currently pending final review at the White House, according to a federal regulatory tracker.

OPT serves as the primary on-ramp for international talent entering the US workforce. Most Silicon Valley and Wall Street firms hire students through OPT before sponsoring them for H-1B or other specialty visas. Industry groups have warned that attaching a six-figure fee to this early-career program would sharply reduce the number of international graduates remaining in the US long-term.

Earlier in August, DHS also added fees of up to $4,500 for applications to extend H-1B workers' stays or transfer employees from overseas offices to the United States.

Enhanced Vetting Reshapes Hiring

Beyond fees, the administration has imposed heightened scrutiny on visa applicants. The State Department has ordered US consulates to review the LinkedIn profiles and resumes of H-1B applicants — and their accompanying family members — for any involvement in content moderation, fact-checking, or what the administration characterizes as suppression of free speech.

"If you uncover evidence an applicant was responsible for, or complicit in, censorship or attempted censorship of protected expression in the US, you should pursue a finding that the applicant is ineligible."

— US State Department cable to all missions

The policy applies to all visa applicants but targets H-1B holders specifically, given their concentration in the technology sector. Companies have reported that the changes are affecting hiring and expansion plans, with some major H-1B users, including Google, moving to increase operations in India rather than navigate the tightening US regime.

Registration Numbers Plunge

The cumulative impact is measurable. Employers registered for about 344,000 H-1B visas last year, down more than 25% from 2024 and fewer than half of the 794,000 sought in 2023, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services. As of late February, only about 70 employers had paid the $100,000 fee, covering a total of 85 visa applications, court filings show.

The H-1B program offers 65,000 visas annually, with an additional 20,000 reserved for workers with advanced degrees. Visas are typically granted for three years and renewable to six.

Legal Challenges and Exemptions

The fee increases face mounting legal challenges. A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing a June ruling by a federal judge who found the original $100,000 fee illegal and blocked its collection. The US Chamber of Commerce, Democratic-led states, and a coalition of unions and employers have filed separate lawsuits challenging the administration's authority to impose the fee without Congressional approval.

The proposed permanent rule does include one significant carve-out: visa applications from hospitals, research institutions, and other nonprofits would be exempt from the six-figure fee. The exemption followed lobbying from hospitals, particularly those in rural areas that struggle to recruit enough domestic medical talent.

India's technology industry association NASSCOM has said it is engaging with US stakeholders over the proposed fee increase, urging the administration to consider the economic benefits the visa program offers companies facing worker shortages. The pending lawsuits could be amended to challenge the new proposed rule once it is finalized.
